summary: Modifies SIP to address problems found in the non-INVITE transaction. The changes reduce the chance of messages losing a race, cut useless network traffic, and improve robustness when network elements stop responding. They update behavior defined in RFC 3261. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Some SIP requests could cause pointless chatter. This memo fixes the rules so devices talk less and cope better when someone goes quiet.

questions: what is a sip non-invite transaction
why is 408 not allowed for non-invite requests
when can a sip element send 100 trying
what does rfc 4320 change in rfc 3261
subtitle: Small changes to SIP's non-INVITE transactions that cut useless messages and stop timeout storms.

tldr.problem: SIP non-INVITE transactions have a fixed duration, so a slow responder can lose a race and be blacklisted, provisional responses can delay recovery, and useless 408 responses can pile up into an O(N^2) storm through N proxies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC forbids non-100 provisional responses, restricts and then requires 100 Trying at set times, forbids 408 responses to non-INVITE requests, and stops proxies from forwarding late or stray non-INVITE responses.
tldr.outcome: Fewer lost races, less wasted traffic and better resistance to flooding. These are normative updates to RFC 3261, and remembering non-responsive destinations is left to future work.

today: RFC 4320 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3261, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The problems it responds to are analyzed in RFC 4321.

sections.title: The Problems with Non-INVITE Transactions
sections.content:
The SIP non-INVITE transaction (NIT) model has a fixed duration, which creates several unpleasant edge cases. The RFC summarizes them, pointing to RFC 4321 for the full analysis.

  • A non-INVITE transaction must complete immediately or risk losing a race.
  • Losing the race makes the requester stop sending traffic to the responder, which is temporarily blacklisted.
  • Provisional responses can delay recovery from lost final responses.
  • The 408 response is useless for a non-INVITE transaction.
  • As transactions through N proxies time out, there can be an O(N^2) storm of useless 408 responses.

This document updates RFC 3261 to improve behavior when these conditions arise.
sections.eli5: SIP requests like this have a strict time limit. If a helper answers a moment late, the asker may give up on them for a while, and lots of pointless late replies can pile up.

sections.title: Action 1: Better Use of Provisional Responses
sections.content:
The first goal is to reduce the chance of losing the race, and to cut useless messaging, when responses are only delayed. Since non-INVITE transactions must complete rapidly, anything beyond "I'm here" can wait for the final response. That minimal message is 100 Trying.

  • Non-100 provisional responses to non-INVITE requests are disallowed, because they waste bandwidth.
  • Sending any provisional before Timer E reaches T2 damages recovery from failure of an unreliable transport (UDP), so 100 Trying is disallowed until then.
  • After Timer E reaches T2, 100 Trying is allowed. It prevents blacklisting of an element that is delaying its final response.
  • Over reliable transports 100 Trying is allowed at any time.

Blacklisting on a late response happens even over reliable transports. Always sending a 100 Trying immediately would only add traffic, so the RFC suggests sending it after the time it would take Timer E to reach T2 on a UDP hop as one reasonable compromise.
sections.eli5: If you need extra time to answer, say "I'm here!" once, and not too early. Don't send a stream of progress reports.

sections.title: Action 2: Ending the Late-Response Storm
sections.content:
A 408 to a non-INVITE request always arrives too late to be useful. The client already knows the transaction timed out, and it cannot do anything with the server's opinion, so the 408 only wastes network resources and feeds the response bombardment.

Late non-INVITE responses arrive after the client transaction's Timer F has fired and the transaction has entered the Terminated state. They cannot be told apart from strays. So the RFC prohibits forwarding stray non-INVITE responses. That ends the storm and also improves a proxy's defenses against malicious users who rely on the RFC 3261 requirement to forward such strays.
sections.eli5: A "you took too long" message that arrives after everyone has already given up helps nobody. So nobody sends it, and nobody passes along answers that come in too late.

sections.title: The Normative Changes to RFC 3261
sections.content:
Section 4 turns the two actions into requirements.

Action 1. A SIP element MUST NOT send a provisional response other than 100 to a non-INVITE request. It MUST NOT send 100 over an unreliable transport such as UDP before the time it takes a client transaction's Timer E to be reset to T2. It MAY send 100 over a reliable transport at any time. Regardless of transport, it MUST send 100 if it has not otherwise responded after that same amount of time.

Action 2. A transaction-stateful SIP element MUST NOT send a 408 to a non-INVITE request, so an element that cannot respond before the transaction expires sends no final response at all. A transaction-stateful proxy MUST NOT send any response to a non-INVITE request unless it has a matching server transaction that is not in the Terminated state, so it will not forward late responses.
sections.eli5: The rules say: only ever say "I'm here" (and only at the right time), never send a "too slow" message, and never pass along answers that come after the deadline.

sections.title: Elements That Never Respond
sections.content:
When an element or network fails, the goals widen: identify non-responsive elements, avoid wrongly labeling responsive ones, and avoid non-responsive ones on later requests.

Action 1 helps with the first two goals. Some response, provisional or final, will almost certainly arrive before the transaction times out, so silence is a safer sign that the peer is unavailable, and the existing rules in RFC 3261 and RFC 3263 for that case apply.

The third goal needs more aggressive protocol changes. Future non-INVITE transactions are likely to fail again unless implementations remember non-responsive destinations between transactions, and standardizing those steps is left to future work.
sections.eli5: The new rules make it easier to tell "slow" from "gone". Remembering who is gone, so you stop asking them, is a job for another day.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says many of these changes also prevent flooding and denial-of-service attacks.

  • Forbidding 408 responses stops proxies from automatically producing a storm of useless responses. An attacker could exploit that by luring user agents into sending non-INVITE requests to a black hole (through social engineering or DNS poisoning) or by selectively dropping responses.
  • Forbidding forwarding of late responses removes a trick where an attacker forges messages that look like late responses. Proxies compliant with RFC 3261 were required to forward them, wasting bandwidth and CPU and potentially overwhelming target user agents, especially those with low-speed connections.

The remaining changes do not affect SIP security.
sections.eli5: Pointless replies could be used to flood someone. Not sending or forwarding them takes that weapon away.
